rv.q: 'Big Fish' mostly makes its hybrid status work, at least in the moments that really matter, such as when Butz and his warm co-star, Kate Baldwin, express their affection for their family.
The show's saving grace is that it knows what it wants to be: a feel-good musical about the importance of family, told with enough theatrical razzle-dazzle to sugar-coat its bitter pill of mortality.
Butz proves he's simply in a league of his own, able to switch from middle-aged to teenager in a snap, offering a complex portrait of a Southern man while avoiding good 'ol boy cliches.
So when audience members around me were dabbing their eyes through the protracted finale, why did I want to take a shower?
Yet the show is hobbled by a major flaw: Andrew Lippa’s thoroughly mediocre score.
So it's crushing to realize, early on, that this gentle, sincere, beautiful-looking show is deadly dull.
Not once did I feel that what I was seeing had been spawned by the teeming mind of Edward Bloom.
But the show built around him is a pulseless bore, and you can see his shoulders sagging from carrying all that weight.
Unfortunately, Andrew Lippa’s score is a hack job stringing one banal non-tune after another.
It’s enchanting, especially once it slows down a bit to catch its breath.
Fantasy wages war with reality in Big Fish, a delightfully old-fashioned musical based on Daniel Wallace's beloved novel.

Wholesomeness gets a bad rap on Broadway these days, usually regarded as the kind of unbearably sweet and inoffensive entertainment that sophisticated theatergoers must endure while taking their conservative grandmas out for a night on the town...
Where “Big Fish” gets stuck in the shallows is with its score, by Andrew Lippa (“The Addams Family”).
Broadway’s new musical fable, “Big Fish,” is a singing version of catch-and-release.

As the sequences of Edward's fantasies play out, however, the father-son story is frequently lost in the whimsicality rather than enhanced by it. It's only near the very end, when Will learns what Edward has accomplished and comes to appreciate the value of a man telling stories, that all the elements properly converge.
Suddenly, they’re not archetypes anymore but rather the stars of some “Best of Broadway” theme-park show.
But the biggest fish in this pond is Butz, who splashes and swims with grace, confidence, and charisma.
In the end, though, this Big Fish lacks the imagination or cohesion to reel you in like one of its hero's yarns.

The rich, gothic mise-en-scène and seamless transitions of the film are replaced with poor quality songs, a slow pace, excessive sentimentality, one-liners that consistently fail to land, a clumsy structure and an ugly set where video imagery is projected onto what look like barn doors.

cn.t: Norbert Leo Butz earns raves in this visually inventive but uneven musical, with Stroman's staging praised while Lippa's score disappoints. Critics find the father-son story heartfelt yet bloated, alternately enchanting and overstuffed.

vs.sum: The Neil Simon Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, although comfort is compromised by tight legroom and narrow seats. The ambiance is appealing with its classic architectural charm, and facilities are average, with typical restroom and concession offerings.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Step-free from street to Orchestra. No elevator.
